synopsis: Across the accident evidence, blind areas and the size mismatch between heavy machines and people or light vehicles are central to the deadliest collisions; although forward run-overs are identified as the deadliest documented pattern, 67% of the 22 US surface-mine blind-area deaths recorded from 2000 to mid-2006 involved victims behind reversing equipment [f2977, f3588, f2984, f2986]. In that dataset, dump trucks were involved in 38% of deaths and front-end loaders in 33%; a 50 t haul truck's front-right blind area extends 18 m or more and grows with truck size [f2985, f3221]. US construction and metal/non-metal mining rules require reverse warnings, specified alternatives or observers when rear visibility is obstructed, with OSHA interpretations accepting cameras only when they genuinely provide the required clear view [f2228, f2237, f2229]. Validation should map blind zones before hardware arrives and build scenarios around each machine model's blind areas, because geometry and sensor placement limit evidence transfer between models; low-speed work may still require relatively large warning zones measured in stopping distances [f5601, f7038, f11551, f11552, f6226]. The proposed geometric methods have verification gaps: ISO 5006 is listed as not verified, and UNECE R159's reported 50 mm cylinder detail was not confirmed against the regulation text [f15219, f5356, f15220].
